column9: To have a good relationship with someone.
column10: Is there anyone at work you don't get on with?
column11: I've always got on well with my neighbours.
column12: He finds it hard to get on with his new boss.

column9: To support or defend a person or idea when they are being attacked or criticized.
column10: Can you recall a time when you had to stand up for a friend?
column11: You must learn to stand up for your own rights.
column12: She always stands up for what she believes in.

column9: To delay someone or something; to rob a place with a weapon.
column10: What would you do if you were in a bank during a hold up?
column11: Sorry I'm late, the traffic held me up.
column12: The construction project was held up by bad weather.

column9: To try to find something or someone.
column10: What is the most important thing you have ever lost and had to look for?
column11: I'm looking for my keys; have you seen them?
column12: She's looking for a new job in marketing.

column9: To lift something; to collect someone; to learn a new skill easily.
column10: How do you remember to pick up everything you need when leaving the house?
column11: I'll pick you up from the station at 6 PM.
column12: He picked up a bit of Spanish while living in Madrid.

column9: To meet someone you know unexpectedly.
column10: Have you ever bumped into someone you hadn't seen in years?
column11: I bumped into an old school friend at the supermarket.
column12: If you bump into Sarah, tell her I said hello.

column9: To remove clothing; (of an aircraft) to leave the ground; to become successful suddenly.
column10: When do you think it's necessary to take off your shoes at someone's house?
column11: The plane took off an hour late.
column12: Her singing career really took off after that performance.

column9: To exercise; to calculate or solve a problem; to have a good result.
column10: How often do you work out, and what exercises do you prefer?
column11: I can't work out the answer to this maths problem.
column12: Don't worry, I'm sure everything will work out in the end.

column9: To stop doing a regular habit; to stop trying.
column10: Have you ever tried to give up a bad habit?
column11: He decided to give up smoking for health reasons.
column12: The puzzle was too difficult, so I gave up.

column9: To become friends again after an argument.
column10: Can you describe a situation where you had to make up with someone after an argument?
column11: They argued yesterday, but they've already made up with each other.
column12: It's always better to make up with your siblings than to stay angry.

column9: To compensate for something lost, missed, or deficient.
column10: What's a good way to make up for missing a friend's important event?
column11: He bought her flowers to make up for forgetting their anniversary.
column12: Nothing can make up for the loss of a loved one.

column9: To wait until you get what you want or demand, refusing to accept anything less.
column10: Have you ever held out for a better offer in a job?
column11: The workers are holding out for a 10% pay rise.
column12: I'm holding out for a sunny day before going to the beach.

column9: To stop a machine or electronic device; to cause someone to lose interest.
column10: Why is it important to turn off the lights when leaving a room?
column11: Please turn off your phone during the film.
column12: The rude waiter really turned me off the restaurant.

column9: To take care of or be in charge of someone or something.
column10: Who is going to look after the cat while we're away?
column11: She looks after her younger brother when her parents work late.
column12: It's important to look after your physical health.

column9: To manage to do something or see someone in a short space of time.
column10: Can you share any tips on how to squeeze in exercise during a busy day?
column11: The doctor is very busy, but she can squeeze you in at 4 PM.
column12: I managed to squeeze in a quick coffee break between meetings.

column9: To finally agree to what someone wants, after refusing for a period of time; to yield to temptation.
column10: Have you ever had to give in to a food craving and then regretted it?
column11: The government refused to give in to the terrorists' demands.
column12: If you give in to your fears, you'll never try anything new.

column9: To gradually relax after doing something that has made you tired or worried.
column10: How do you wind down before bedtime to promote a good night's sleep?
column11: I like to wind down with a good book after a long day at the office.
column12: The party started to wind down around 2 AM.

column9: To consume less of something or reduce spending.
column10: Have you ever tried cutting back on caffeine intake to improve your sleep?
column11: We need to cut back on our expenses if we want to save for a holiday.
column12: He was advised by his doctor to cut back on sugar.

column9: To create a state of equilibrium or equal proportions.
column10: How do you balance out work responsibilities with personal activities?
column11: The sweet flavor of the dessert balances out the tartness of the fruit.
column12: We need to balance out the team with more experienced players.

column9: To do or use less of something (synonymous with cut back on).
column10: Do you think you have to cut down on screen time before bedtime?
column11: I'm trying to cut down on the amount of meat I eat.
column12: The doctor told him to cut down on smoking.

column9: To become confused about where one is and which way to go.
column10: I get lost so easily; I completely lose my sense of direction.
column11: When he walked out of the subway station, he temporarily lost his sense of direction.
column12: Without a map or GPS, it's easy to lose your sense of direction in a new city.

column9: To go down the wrong path or road.
column10: I assume one thing is next to another, and then I take a wrong turn.
column11: We took a wrong turn and ended up miles away from the hotel.
column12: If you take a wrong turn, the GPS will automatically reroute you.

column9: Used as a mild swear word to express anger or annoyance, or for emphasis (similar to 'freaking' or 'bloody').
column10: Where's the flippin' Louvre gone?
column11: That was a flippin' good movie!
column12: I've been waiting here for flippin' ages.

column9: To trick someone into making a mistake or showing they are doing something wrong.
column10: It's easy for Paris to catch you out when you think you know where you are.
column11: The tricky exam question was designed to catch students out.
column12: He tried to catch her out in a lie during the interview.

column9: To forget what one was talking or thinking about.
column10: Wait, I completely lost my train of thought. What was I saying?
column11: The phone rang and made me lose my train of thought.
column12: I lost my train of thought when someone interrupted me mid-sentence.

column9: An expression asking someone to be patient while you do something or find the right words.
column10: Bear with me a second while I check my map.
column11: Bear with me, my computer is running a bit slow today.
column12: If you'll just bear with me, I'll explain everything.

column9: To find someone or something after a thorough search.
column10: I need to track down my friend before the concert starts.
column11: The police managed to track down the suspect in another city.
column12: It took me hours to track down the rare book I was looking for.

column9: To talk to someone you haven't seen for a while and find out what they've been doing.
column10: We went for a coffee to catch up on all the news.
column11: It was great to catch up with you after so many years.
column12: Let's catch up over lunch next week.

column9: Several times; many times.
column10: I've recorded walk and talk episodes a bunch of times before.
column11: I've watched that movie a bunch of times, I love it.
column12: He tried calling her a bunch of times, but she didn't answer.

column9: To begin to sleep, especially unintentionally or easily.
column10: I was so tired I just dropped off to sleep on the sofa.
column11: She dropped off to sleep in the middle of the lecture.
column12: I struggle to drop off to sleep if there's any noise in the house.

column9: To gradually fall asleep, usually in a peaceful way.
column10: It's lovely to just sit here with the breeze on my face and drift off to sleep.
column11: He drifted off to sleep while listening to the podcast.
column12: The gentle rocking of the boat helped me drift off to sleep.

column9: To fall asleep very quickly, almost instantly.
column10: As soon as my head hit the pillow, I was out like a light.
column11: The baby was exhausted and was out like a light within minutes.
column12: After the marathon, he was out like a light on the couch.

column9: To sleep more than usual in order to compensate for a previous lack of sleep.
column10: I need the weekend to catch up on sleep after this busy week.
column11: She stayed in bed until noon to catch up on sleep.
column12: If you don't catch up on sleep, you'll feel lethargic all day.

column9: To become fatter or heavier.
column10: I seem to have put on weight over the Christmas holidays.
column11: If you eat too much junk food, you'll put on weight.
column12: He put on a lot of weight when he stopped exercising.

column9: To stop eating or doing something completely, usually for health reasons.
column10: I need to completely cut out snacking between meals.
column11: She cut out dairy from her diet.
column12: You should cut out sugar if you want to lose weight quickly.

column9: Reasons relating to the food a person eats, often for health or medical purposes.
column10: I haven't had to give up anything for certain dietary reasons.
column11: She requires a special meal on the flight for dietary reasons.
column12: He avoided the cake due to dietary reasons.

column9: A deliberate and intentional attempt to do something.
column10: It was a conscious effort to cut down on the take-away curries.
column11: You have to make a conscious effort to improve your pronunciation.
column12: He made a conscious effort to be more polite to his colleagues.

column9: To be too lazy or lacking motivation to do something.
column10: I ordered curry because I couldn't be bothered to cook.
column11: She couldn't be bothered to walk to the shops, so she drove.
column12: I should tidy my room, but I just can't be bothered right now.

column9: A situation that is annoying because it involves doing something difficult or complicated.
column10: Cooking dinner just seemed like too much of a hassle.
column11: Getting a visa for that country is a real hassle.
column12: Save yourself the hassle and book your tickets online.

column9: A temporary structure on the outside of a building, used by workers while building, repairing, or cleaning it.
column10: I'm standing in front of Notre Dame and it is covered in scaffolding.
column11: The builders put up scaffolding around the house to fix the roof.
column12: The scaffolding collapsed during the strong storm.

column9: A tall metal structure with a long horizontal part, used for lifting and moving heavy objects.
column10: There are huge cranes all around the cathedral building site.
column11: The crane lifted the steel beams to the top of the skyscraper.
column12: We watched the construction cranes moving across the city skyline.

column9: To start burning.
column10: A few years ago, Notre Dame caught fire and it was devastating.
column11: Don't leave the towel near the stove, it might catch fire.
column12: The dry grass caught fire easily in the summer heat.

column9: Doing things or arriving later than planned or scheduled.
column10: I just got a message from Paul who says he's running late.
column11: I can't talk right now, I'm running late for a meeting.
column12: The trains are running late today because of the snow.

column9: To hurry up.
column10: I'm going to have to get my skates on if I want to catch the train.
column11: Get your skates on, or we'll miss the start of the film!
column12: We need to get our skates on to finish this project by Friday.

column9: To make a special effort to do something, especially to help someone or achieve a goal.
column10: Being healthy can be a question of trying to go out of your way to get more exercise.
column11: He went out of his way to make sure the new employee felt welcome.
column12: I went out of my way to buy her favourite cake for her birthday.

column9: The use of willpower to overcome physical problems or unappealing tasks.
column10: Pushing through the fatigue during the marathon was a question of mind over matter.
column11: If you're scared of heights, skydiving is a true test of mind over matter.
column12: He survived the freezing cold temperatures using mind over matter.

column9: To make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse.
column10: Caffeine exacerbates my stress, so I try to avoid it.
column11: Scratching the mosquito bite will only exacerbate the itchiness.
column12: His angry comments exacerbated an already tense situation.

column9: To no longer feel hungry, often due to stress, illness, or shock.
column10: When I'm very stressed, I tend to lose my appetite completely.
column11: She lost her appetite after hearing the bad news.
column12: The side effects of the medication made him lose his appetite.

column9: Having little energy; feeling unwilling and unable to do anything.
column10: After eating the massive burger, I felt full, lethargic, and sleepy.
column11: The hot weather makes me feel lethargic and lazy.
column12: He's been feeling lethargic ever since he caught the flu.

column9: Causing someone to feel happier and more relaxed or to be more healthy.
column10: Stroking a cat or a dog can be very therapeutic.
column11: Listening to classical music is a highly therapeutic experience for me.
column12: She finds gardening to be a therapeutic hobby after a stressful week.

column9: A shallow box containing absorbent material for a cat to use as an indoor toilet.
column10: We can't get a cat because we don't know where we would put the litter tray.
column11: You need to clean the cat's litter tray every day to prevent smells.
column12: The kitten quickly learned how to use the litter tray.

column9: A small hole with a door in a door or wall, for a cat to go in and out.
column10: We'd need to get a cat flap installed so the cat could come in and out.
column11: The cat stood by the cat flap waiting to be let outside.
column12: A stray cat entered the kitchen through our cat flap.

column9: Requiring too much effort or causing too many problems relative to the benefit it provides.
column10: To be honest, I think getting a pet right now is more complicated than it's worth.
column11: Fixing that old car is going to be more complicated than it's worth.
column12: I considered disputing the small fee, but decided it was more complicated than it's worth.

column9: To adopt a diet and lifestyle that avoids all animal products.
column10: Have you ever considered going vegan for health or ethical reasons?
column11: She decided to go vegan after watching a documentary about the meat industry.
column12: Going vegan can be challenging at first, but many find it rewarding.
